lessons.title: Lesson 1: When protected farming pays, and when it does not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the five conditions for protected farming on your own farm and decide whether to go ahead.
This lesson builds toward: For your own farm, you will check the five conditions for protected farming (water, market, skills, capital and climate) and decide whether to go ahead, giving a yes or no for each with a reason.
Protected farming means growing a crop under a cover: a greenhouse with plastic sheeting and insect net, a shade-net house, or a low or walk-in tunnel. Done well, it keeps off heavy rain, hail and many insects, cuts some diseases, and gives higher, cleaner, more regular yields of high-value crops such as tomatoes, capsicum and cucumbers.
It does not suit everyone. A 2017 review of protected cultivation in sub-Saharan Africa found it is not suitable in every climate and still needs other pest controls, and that a lack of skills, technical support and finance stops many smallholders. Many greenhouses in Kenya, Nigeria and Ghana stand empty after one or two crops.
Check five conditions before you spend money. Water: a reliable, clean supply all year, because the crop gets no rain. Market: buyers who will take your produce every week at a fair price, such as a hotel, supermarket, school or market traders, not just "the market". Skills: you or a worker trained in fertigation, pruning and scouting, and an agronomist you can call. Capital: money for the structure, the first crop and some months of running costs, without risking your family's food. Climate: in very hot lowlands a closed greenhouse can overheat, so a shade net or a well-ventilated design may suit better.
Step by step:
- Water: is there a reliable, clean supply all year?
- Market: who will buy every week, and at what price?
- Skills: who will run fertigation, pruning and scouting, and which agronomist can you call?
- Capital: can you pay for the structure, the first crop and running costs without risking food money?
- Climate: will a closed structure overheat where you are?
- Decide: go ahead, start smaller, or not yet.
Words to know:
- Protected farming: growing crops under a cover such as a greenhouse, shade net or tunnel.
- Greenhouse: a frame covered with plastic sheeting and insect net, with vents for air.
- Shade net: a net that cuts some sunlight and heat and keeps out some insects and birds.
- Tunnel: a curved frame covered with plastic or net; low tunnels cover a bed, walk-in tunnels cover a plot.
Official sources:
- Nordey and others (2017): Protected cultivation of vegetable crops in sub-Saharan Africa: limits and prospects for smallholders. A review (Agronomy for Sustainable Development)
- FAO: Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Crops: Principles for Mediterranean Climate Areas (Plant Production and Protection Paper 217)
Try it now: Write the five conditions down and answer each one for your farm with yes or no and a reason. Then write your decision: go ahead, start smaller, or not yet, and what you would need to change.
You can now check the five conditions for protected farming and decide whether it suits your farm now.

check.q: Which is the strongest sign you are ready for a greenhouse?
options: A seller says it pays in three months
Your neighbour bought one
You have water all year and a buyer who takes tomatoes every week
You have seen photos online
check.why: Reliable water and a steady buyer are two of the five conditions that make it pay.

check.q: You farm in a very hot lowland area. What should you check first?
options: Whether a closed greenhouse will overheat, and if a shade net suits better
Only the colour of the plastic
Nothing; heat is good for all crops
Whether you can grow without water
check.why: Closed structures trap heat; in hot areas, ventilation or shade nets may suit better.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greenhouses, shade nets and tunnels: options, costs and sellers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare at least three structure quotes and check each seller's claims.
This lesson builds toward: When choosing a structure, you will compare greenhouse, shade-net or tunnel quotes and check each seller's claims, using at least three quotes and asking for references and a written warranty.
The main options: a greenhouse (wood or steel frame with UV-treated plastic on the roof and insect net on the sides) gives the most protection and costs the most. A shade-net house costs less, runs cooler and suits hot areas and crops such as capsicum and leafy vegetables, but does not keep off rain. Walk-in or low tunnels are the cheapest way to start and learn. Steel lasts longer than wood but costs more; treated wood can work if termites are controlled. The plastic cover wears out after some years, so ask how long its UV protection is guaranteed.
Costs vary widely by size, material, country and what is included, so get at least three written quotes for the same size and compare line by line: frame, cover and net, doors, drip system, water tank, nursery, installation, training and after-sales visits. For example (invented figures, only to show the method), quote A of KES 380,000 may include drip and training while quote B of KES 300,000 does not, so B is not really cheaper.
Be careful with sellers who over-promise. Warning signs: guaranteed yields or income, "pays back in one season", a "buy-back" promise with no written contract, pressure to pay a big deposit today, no farmers you can visit, no written warranty, and kits sold with no training or water plan. Ask to visit two farmers who have used the seller's structure for at least two seasons. Get the warranty, delivery date and what is included in writing, read the whole contract, and ask a trusted adviser before you pay.
Step by step:
- Choose the size you can manage and water.
- Ask at least three sellers for written quotes for the same size.
- Compare line by line: frame, cover, net, drip, tank, nursery, installation, training, after-sales.
- Ask each seller for references and visit two farmers using their structure.
- Get the warranty, delivery date and contents in writing; read it all and ask an adviser.
Words to know:
- UV-treated plastic: greenhouse plastic made to resist the sun's ultraviolet light so it lasts longer.
- Insect net: a fine net on the sides and vents that keeps out many insects but lets air through.
- Quote: a written price from a seller showing exactly what is included.
- Warranty: a written promise from the seller to repair or replace parts that fail within a set time.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Crops: Principles for Mediterranean Climate Areas (Plant Production and Protection Paper 217)
- Nordey and others (2017): Protected cultivation of vegetable crops in sub-Saharan Africa: limits and prospects for smallholders. A review (Agronomy for Sustainable Development)
Try it now: Ask at least three sellers or builders near you for written quotes for the same size of structure. Put them in a table, line by line, and mark what each leaves out. Write the questions you will ask each seller, including two farmers you can visit.
You can now compare structure quotes line by line and check a seller's claims before you pay.

check.q: A seller guarantees 10 tonnes of tomatoes and payback in one season, if you pay a deposit today. What do you do?
options: Pay at once before the offer ends
Pay half and decide later
Sign without reading
Treat it as a warning sign, ask for references and written terms, and compare quotes
check.why: Guaranteed yields and pressure to pay today are classic signs of over-promising.

check.q: Quote B is cheaper than quote A but has no drip system or training. What is true?
options: B is clearly the better deal
B may cost more once you add what it leaves out
Drip and training are never needed
Quotes cannot be compared
check.why: Compare line by line; missing items must be bought separately.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing a crop and raising clean seedlings
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a crop and variety for your structure and plan a clean nursery and transplanting.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop you choose, you will plan the variety, nursery, transplanting and drip fertigation with an agronomist, as a dated plan for one crop cycle.
The most common protected crops are tomatoes, capsicum (sweet pepper) and cucumbers. Tomatoes have the biggest market but also the biggest pest and disease risk, including Tuta absoluta. Capsicum sells well to hotels and supermarkets, especially coloured ones, and is slower to start. Cucumbers grow fast and give quick cash. Choose by your buyer first: which crop, colour and size they will take every week.
Use varieties bred for greenhouses. Many greenhouse tomatoes are indeterminate (they keep growing and are trained up a string for many months), and many greenhouse cucumbers set fruit without bees. Seed of these varieties can be costly, so buy sealed, certified seed from a registered dealer (KEPHIS certifies seed in Kenya) and do not save seed from hybrids.
Raise seedlings in a clean nursery: seedling trays with a clean growing medium (not soil from the field), under insect net, with careful watering. Many farmers buy seedlings from a licensed propagator, which saves time but must be a clean, trusted source. Transplant strong, healthy seedlings with no pests in the cool evening, at the spacing your agronomist gives, and water them in at once. Plan the dates: sowing, transplanting, first harvest and last harvest, so your buyer gets produce on time.
Step by step:
- Ask your buyer which crop, colour and size they will take weekly.
- Choose a greenhouse variety; buy sealed, certified seed.
- Raise seedlings in trays with clean medium under insect net, or buy from a licensed propagator.
- Transplant strong, pest-free seedlings in the evening at the agronomist's spacing.
- Write the dates: sowing, transplanting, first and last harvest.
Words to know:
- Capsicum: sweet pepper; green, red, yellow or orange.
- Indeterminate: a tomato type that keeps growing and fruiting for months; it is trained up a string.
- Growing medium: a clean mix (for example cocopeat) used instead of soil to raise seedlings.
- Propagator: a nursery business that raises and sells seedlings.
Official sources:
- Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS): certified seed and seedlings
- icipe: Insect of the Month: Tomato leafminer, Tuta absoluta
Try it now: Ask one buyer what crop, colour and size they would take each week. Choose your crop and a greenhouse variety, and write the dates for sowing (or buying seedlings), transplanting, first harvest and last harvest.
You can now choose a protected crop by your buyer's needs and plan clean seedlings and transplanting.

check.q: What should decide which crop you grow in your greenhouse first?
options: What your buyer will take every week
The crop with the nicest seed packet
Whatever the neighbour grows
The cheapest seed
check.why: A steady buyer is what makes a protected crop pay.

check.q: Where should greenhouse seedlings be raised?
options: In open field soil next to old tomatoes
Under a tree with no net
In trays with a clean medium under insect net, or from a licensed propagator
Anywhere; pests do not matter in a greenhouse
check.why: Clean seedlings stop pests and diseases entering the structure with the crop.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drip fertigation basics
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe how a drip fertigation system works and plan its daily checks with an agronomist.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop you choose, you will plan the variety, nursery, transplanting and drip fertigation with an agronomist, as a dated plan for one crop cycle.
Fertigation means giving fertilizer through the drip system, dissolved in the irrigation water, so each plant gets a little food and water at its roots every day. It saves water and fertilizer and keeps leaves dry, which helps against disease. Drip systems, pumps and solar options are taught in "Irrigation and Water Management"; this lesson covers what is different under cover.
A simple system has a water tank, a filter, a way to add the fertilizer (a dosing tank or an injector), mainline pipes and drip lines with emitters at each plant. Use only water-soluble fertilizers made for fertigation. The recipe changes with the crop and its stage (seedling, flowering, fruiting) and with your water and soil, so get it from an agronomist, a soil and water test or the fertilizer supplier's technical staff. Never guess, and never mix products in the same tank unless the agronomist says they can be mixed.
Check the system every day: the filter is clean, every emitter drips, no lines leak, and the soil around the plants is moist, not soaked. Many growers use a cheap EC meter to check that the fertilizer strength in the water is what the agronomist set, and a pH meter or strips. Flush the lines with clean water as advised, so salts and fertilizer do not block the emitters. Write each day's water and feed in a record.
Step by step:
- Get a feeding plan by crop stage from an agronomist or soil and water test.
- Use only water-soluble fertilizers for fertigation; mix only as advised.
- Each day: clean filter, check emitters drip and lines do not leak.
- Check the strength with an EC meter and pH as the agronomist set.
- Flush lines as advised; record water and feed each day.
Words to know:
- Fertigation: giving fertilizer dissolved in irrigation water through a drip system.
- Emitter: the small outlet on a drip line that releases water at each plant.
- EC meter: a small meter that measures how much dissolved fertilizer (salt) is in the water.
- Flushing: running clean water through the lines to clear salts and blockages.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Crops: Principles for Mediterranean Climate Areas (Plant Production and Protection Paper 217)
Try it now: Draw your drip fertigation system from tank to plants and label each part. Then write a daily checklist (filter, emitters, leaks, EC, pH, soil moisture, record) and the questions you will ask your agronomist about the feeding plan for each crop stage.
You can now describe a drip fertigation system, plan its feeding with an agronomist and run its daily checks.

check.q: Where should your fertigation recipe come from?
options: A guess from the colour of the leaves
An agronomist, soil and water test or the supplier's technical staff
The same recipe for every crop and stage
Whatever is cheapest that week
check.why: The recipe depends on crop, stage, water and soil, so it must come from expert advice.

check.q: Several plants are wilting while others are fine. What do you check first?
options: Whether their emitters are blocked and the filter is clean
Add more fertilizer to the tank
Remove the insect net
Water from above with a hose
check.why: Blocked emitters are a common reason some plants get no water or feed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Managing heat, humidity, pests and hygiene
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run a daily and weekly routine for heat, humidity, pests and hygiene in your structure.
This lesson builds toward: Once the crop is planted, you will run a daily and weekly routine for heat, humidity, pests and hygiene, covering vents, scouting, traps and entry rules every week.
Heat and humidity are the biggest day-to-day problems under cover in the tropics. A closed greenhouse can get much hotter than outside, and hot, still, wet air brings fungal diseases such as late blight and grey mould. Open the side and roof vents in the morning and close them in the evening as needed, keep leaves dry by watering only through the drip, prune old lower leaves and side shoots so air moves, and do not overcrowd. A shade net over the roof in the hottest months can help. Keep a cheap thermometer inside and write the readings.
Insect nets keep out many pests, but the ones that get in multiply fast with no rain or natural enemies to stop them: whiteflies, thrips, aphids, spider mites and, in tomatoes, Tuta absoluta. In the soil, root-knot nematodes are a common problem in long-used greenhouses. Scout every plant row weekly, hang yellow sticky cards for whiteflies and aphids and blue ones for thrips, and use pheromone traps for Tuta absoluta. Use the IPM steps; if a pesticide is needed, use only one registered for your crop (PCPB in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, the EPA in Ghana), follow the label and its pre-harvest interval, and wear protective equipment, because you will pick fruit in a closed space often.
Hygiene keeps pests and disease out. Use a double door so one is always closed, and a footbath at the entrance. Limit visitors, and have workers wash hands and wear clean clothes. Remove sick plants and fallen leaves and fruit in a sealed bag, keep the area around the structure weeded, repair holes in the net at once, and clean tools. Between crops, remove all plant waste and clean the structure before you plant again.
Step by step:
- Every morning: open vents; read the thermometer; check for wet leaves.
- Every evening: close vents as needed; record temperature.
- Weekly: scout every row; count sticky-card and pheromone-trap catches.
- Weekly: prune lower leaves and side shoots; remove sick plants and waste in a sealed bag.
- Always: double door closed, footbath, limited visitors, clean tools, repair net holes.
Words to know:
- Ventilation: letting air move through the structure through vents to lower heat and humidity.
- Humidity: how much water vapour is in the air; high humidity helps fungal diseases.
- Root-knot nematode: a tiny worm in the soil that makes swellings on roots and weakens plants.
- Footbath: a shallow tray of disinfectant at the entrance to clean boots.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Crops: Principles for Mediterranean Climate Areas (Plant Production and Protection Paper 217)
- icipe: Insect of the Month: Tomato leafminer, Tuta absoluta
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya)
- National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC, Nigeria)
- Environmental Protection Authority (Ghana)
Try it now: Write a one-page routine for your structure: what you do every morning and evening, what you do every week (scouting, traps, pruning, waste) and your entry rules (doors, footbath, visitors). Put it on the door.
You can now run a daily and weekly routine for heat, humidity, pests and hygiene in a protected structure.

check.q: It is hot and humid inside and you see grey mould starting. What helps most?
options: Water the leaves with a hose
Close all vents all day
Plant more plants closer
Open the vents, keep leaves dry and prune lower leaves for air
check.why: Moving air and dry leaves slow fungal diseases.

check.q: Why use a double door at the greenhouse entrance?
options: To look modern
So one door is always closed and fewer insects get in
To keep workers inside
It lets in more heat
check.why: With one door always shut, insects cannot fly straight in.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The business case: gross margin and payback
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost, income, gross margin and payback period for one protected crop.
This lesson builds toward: Given your quotes and market prices, you will calculate the cost, income, gross margin and payback period for the crop, and test what happens if the price falls by a quarter.
A business case shows, with numbers, whether the structure can pay for itself before it wears out. You need two kinds of cost. The investment is what you pay once: the structure, drip system, tank and installation. Running costs come every crop cycle: seed or seedlings, fertilizer, crop protection, labour, water and power, transport, packaging and market fees.
Gross margin per cycle = income (expected kg sold x price per kg) - running costs. Payback period = investment / gross margin per year. Invented example in KES, only to practise the method: investment KES 400,000; one tomato cycle a year; expected sales 4,000 kg at KES 40 = KES 160,000; running costs KES 90,000; gross margin KES 70,000 a year. Payback = 400,000 / 70,000 = about 5.7 years. If the seller says the cover lasts about 4 years, this case does not pay back before you must replace it. That is a red flag, not a reason to borrow more.
Now test it. If the price falls by a quarter (KES 30 instead of 40), income becomes KES 120,000, the margin KES 30,000 and payback over 13 years. Prices for tomatoes swing hard by season, so test a bad price, a lower yield and a lost crop. Then look for ways to improve it: a smaller or cheaper structure, a contract with a buyer, two cycles a year, a higher-value crop such as coloured capsicum, or sharing the cost in a group. The same arithmetic works in NGN, GHS or XOF: a grower near Dakar in Senegal does the same sums in CFA francs. Use your own quotes and prices, keep real records once you start, and ask a trusted adviser before you borrow or sign.
Step by step:
- Add up the investment from your chosen quote.
- List running costs for one cycle.
- Income = expected kg sold x price per kg (from your buyer).
- Gross margin = income - running costs; per year = margin x cycles per year.
- Payback = investment / gross margin per year; compare with the life of the cover.
- Test a price fall of a quarter, a lower yield and a lost crop.
Words to know:
- Investment: money paid once to set up, such as the structure and drip system.
- Running costs: money spent every crop cycle, such as seedlings, fertilizer, labour and transport.
- Gross margin: income minus running costs for one cycle or one year.
- Payback period: how long the gross margin takes to repay the investment.
Official sources:
- Nordey and others (2017): Protected cultivation of vegetable crops in sub-Saharan Africa: limits and prospects for smallholders. A review (Agronomy for Sustainable Development)
Try it now: Final task: write your protected-farming business case for one crop: your five conditions, the structure with three quotes compared and seller checks done, the crop and variety, your nursery and fertigation plan, your weekly routine, and the investment, running costs, income, gross margin, payback period, and the payback if the price falls by a quarter.
You can now calculate the gross margin and payback period for a protected crop and test it against a price fall.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Does it suit me? The five conditions are missing or answered without reasons. Water, market, skills, capital and climate are each answered yes or no with a reason, and a clear decision is written. A missing condition has a plan to fix it, such as a named buyer or a water test. Structure and seller checks One quote only, or a seller's promises are taken without checking. At least three quotes compared line by line, with references asked for and the warranty and contents in writing. Two reference farmers were visited and their real results are noted. Crop and fertigation plan No crop timetable, or the feeding plan is a guess. Crop and variety chosen by the buyer's needs, with dated nursery, transplanting and harvest, and a feeding plan from an agronomist or test with daily drip checks. The plan includes EC and pH targets set by the agronomist and a daily record sheet. Climate, pest and hygiene routine No routine, or pests are handled only by spraying. A daily and weekly routine for vents, scouting, traps, pruning, waste and entry rules, with only registered products used as the label says. The routine is posted on the door and has been followed and recorded for at least two weeks. Numbers and payback No numbers, or the gross margin or payback is wrong. Investment, running costs, income, gross margin and payback are correct, compared with the cover's life, and a quarter price fall is tested. Also tests a lower yield and a lost crop, and lists changes that would make the case stronger. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the business case and check it again with an agronomist or trusted adviser before you invest.

check.q: Investment is 300,000 and the gross margin is 100,000 a year. What is the payback period?
options: 1 year
30 years
3 years
100 years

check.q: Your payback is 6 years but the cover lasts about 4. What does this tell you?
options: The case does not pay back in time; change the plan or do not invest yet
It is fine; borrow more
Payback does not matter
Buy a second greenhouse
check.why: If the cover wears out before payback, you lose money unless the plan changes.
